title: Geo-Arbitrage Relocation Calculator
description: Quantify the real financial impact of relocating to a cheaper city while keeping a remote job: disposable income change, relocation payback period, and your salary's true purchasing power.
methodSummary: Target Living Cost = Current Living Cost × (Target Index ÷ Current Index) — your spending rescaled to the cheaper city.
Disposable Income Change = (Target Salary − Target Living Cost) − (Current Salary − Current Living Cost).
Payback = One-Time Relocation Cost ÷ Monthly Disposable Gain.
Real Income = Target Salary × (Current Index ÷ Target Index), i.e. what your new pay is worth at your old city's price level.
assumptions: Cost-of-living indices are relative numbers (e.g. Numbeo or your own basket) where a higher value means a more expensive city.
Living costs are assumed to scale roughly with the index ratio; one-off luxuries and fixed debts are not rescaled.
If your remote employer cuts pay for the cheaper location, enter that lower figure as the salary after the move.
insights: The biggest geo-arbitrage wins come from holding a high-cost-city salary while paying low-cost-city prices — disposable income, not headline salary, is what actually grows.
A pay cut can still be worth it: dropping 15% salary to move somewhere 35% cheaper usually leaves you with more money in your pocket each month.
Watch the payback period — high moving, deposit, and furnishing costs can take a year or more to recoup, so a short planned stay can wipe out the gain.

faqs.q: Where do I find a cost-of-living index?
faqs.a: Numbeo, Expatistan, and many salary sites publish city indices. Any consistent source works as long as you use the same scale for both cities — what matters is the ratio between them, not the absolute number.

faqs.q: What counts as my 'annual living cost'?
faqs.a: Add up what you actually spend in a year on rent, food, transport, utilities and discretionary items. Exclude savings and one-off purchases for the cleanest comparison.

faqs.q: My employer wants to cut my pay if I move. Is it still worth it?
faqs.a: Often yes. Enter the reduced salary as 'Salary After Move'. If the city is cheaper by a larger percentage than the pay cut, your disposable income still rises.

faqs.q: Why is the payback period shown as ∞?
faqs.a: That happens when the move does not increase your monthly disposable income, so there is nothing to recoup the relocation cost. Financially, the move does not pay for itself.

faqs.q: What is 'real income in current-city terms'?
faqs.a: It translates your post-move salary back into the price level of your current city, so you can compare like-for-like. If it is higher than your current salary, your purchasing power improved.
Not directly. If moving changes your tax jurisdiction, adjust the salary figures to net-of-tax amounts, or treat the tax difference as part of your living cost.

faqs.q: What about currency differences for international moves?
faqs.a: Use the calculator's currency selector and convert both salary and living costs into the same currency first, so the index ratio is the only thing driving the comparison.

useCases: Decide whether to relocate for a remote job
Compare disposable income across two cities
Estimate how fast a move pays for itself
richContent:
Worked example: a hypothetical relocation

Assume annual salary stays $70,000, current spending is $45,000 and user-supplied indices are 125 and 75. Modeled destination spending is $27,000, a reduction of $18,000. At $6,000 relocation cost, the modeled payback is four months.

These are invented scenario inputs, not verified city data. The difference is before tax; it is not spendable income until taxes and omitted costs are accounted for. A lower index does not imply permission to work in a country or that your employer will retain your salary.

A pay cut with a long payback

With salary falling from $150,000 to $120,000, spending of $90,000 and an index ratio of 65 / 100, modeled destination spending is $58,500. The annual difference improves by only $1,500. A $10,000 move takes 80 months to recover under those assumptions.

Test housing separately, use consistent same-period indices and compare actual after-tax budgets before treating either scenario as a practical option.
resultNote: Enter both salaries and all money amounts in one currency. Results are before tax; the index does not estimate rent, visas, healthcare or a local salary. Use your own current budget and consistent indices.
